Equivocate

ih-KWIV-uh-kayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To equivocate to use unclear, evasive wording intentionally, especially to avoid committing to a position or to mislead.

Rather than admit the product had failed, the CEO equivocated in every interview that week.

Worked Example

The spokesperson equivocated for ten minutes, using so many qualifiers that no one could tell if the merger was actually happening.

Piling on qualifiers until no one can tell what's true is exactly equivocating.

How Equivocate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

waffle

waffle: avoid giving a direct answer or committing to a position

hedge

hedge: avoid a firm commitment through unclear wording

Antonyms

clarify

clarify: make a statement fully clear

How Strong Is It? — qualify → equivocate → double-talk

qualify vs. equivocate

qualify vs. equivocate: To qualify a statement means adding a small limit or condition, an ordinary part of careful speech; equivocate means burying the truth under SO MANY qualifiers that nothing clear remains.

double-talk vs. equivocate

double-talk vs. equivocate: Double-talk pushes the same idea further into intentional nonsense or contradiction, while equivocate can be quieter -- technically true wording that still avoids a real answer.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of equivocate.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — equi-

prefix — equi-: equal (Latin (aequus))

root — voc

root — voc: voice, call (Latin (vox, vocis))

suffix — -ate

suffix — -ate: to make, to do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Equivocate combines Latin aequus ('equal') + vox ('voice') -- literally 'of equal voice,' describing words that carry two equally possible meanings at once.

Use the root in a new word: voice

Use the root in a new word: voice: The same vox root gives us the everyday word voice itself -- both words are built on that same root for speaking or being heard.

Root Check

Word Choice

Equivocate focuses on intentionally UNCLEAR WORDING chosen to avoid commitment, distinct from Prevaricate (taught in this same unit), which focuses on the broader ACT of evading a direct question by any means, not just wording.
